newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila aide says no fear of new Zaire dictatorship.
newsitem.headline: Kabila aide says no fear of new Zaire dictatorship.

text.p: The world need have no fear that Laurent Kabila will install his own dictatorship after defeating the one-man-rule government of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, a senior Kabila official said on Wednesday.
"Of course there should be elections, otherwise we would not have fought for so long," said Bizima Karaha, foreign affairs spokesman for Kabila's rebel movement.
But the new rulers had no intention of being stampeded by international pressure into elections for which the country was not prepared, Karaha added.
Asked when voting would take place, he replied: "Very soon, when conditions are there for free and fair elections."

"You must remember that there have been elections in this country but they didn't solve the problems of this country," he added, referring to the sham, heavily manipulated voting permitted under Mobutu.
The last elections took place 13 years ago, in 1984.

The United States and other powers are pressing Kabila, who proclaimed himself president of the renamed Democratic Republic of Congo after his troops took Kinshasa at the weekend, to proceed as quickly as possible to a democratic vote and a broad-based government.

But Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) says the 47 million people of Africa's third largest country must be "politically reawakened" and re-educated before they can be called on to vote.
The revolution was now in its second phase, the construction phase, Karaha said. "You must understand that this can't go as fast as the military phase."

"We want free and fair elections everbody should be proud of and participate in. We don't want a pseudo-election, in the same way that we don't want a pseudo-democracy," he told reporters. "We want a real one, a genuine democracy."
Karaha dismissed concerns voiced by some commentators that Kabila could turn out to be another Mobutu.
"It's impossible, it's impossible. We would not have fought. We hate dictatorship," he said.
"Before I was born there was a dictatorship regime so you will understand that I want to see something else than a dictatorship."
Some foreign commentators, and some media outlets of parties long opposed to Mobutu, suggest Kabila might establish one-party rule, which could easily evolve into one-man rule.
"Kinshasa did not give you (Kabila) a blank cheque," said a leading opposition newspaper under a banner headline welcoming the revolutionary army into the capital.
But Karaha, echoing other AFDL officials, said his country and the watching world must look at results and be patient:
"We know there are many challenges ahead but we have achieved the first objective, which is the freedom of our people."
